Au moins aussi acclamé à sa sortie, ce second opus a le mérite d'être divertissant, mais à l'inverse du premier qui était une montée en puissance sur tous les plans, plus les enjeux multiversels prennent du poids, et moins il convainc. Spider-Man : Across the Spider-Verse est bien meilleur lorsqu'il se concentre sur l'intime, même s'il demeure à ce sujet très classique. D'ailleurs, j'ai bien cru que je le préférerais à en juger par son introduction, plus aboutie que celle du précédent, mais la suite m'a déçu. Il est très frustrant de regarder une œuvre qui s'étend sur autant de temps pour ne pas avoir le droit à une vraie fin, fut-elle ouverte. Sur le plan visuel, on est dans la continuité, avec un peu plus de variété issue de l'exploration du multivers. Toutefois, je regrette l'inclusion de live action qui me sort totalement du film. Ponctuellement, certains plans continuent de me gêner par leur façon de trancher avec d'autres mais je dois dire que cela a moins été le cas qu'auparavant. C'est peut-être une question d'habitude, mais je pense surtout que celui-ci est techniquement plus abouti. Quoi que je sois critique, cela reste à des années lumières des bouses super-heroïques que nous sert Marvel à son habitude. Le moment est plaisant mais hormis toute la séquence où Gwen et Miles se retrouvent puis papotent en se collant sur les bâtiments — qui est superbe — je ne sais pas si j'en retiendrais grand chose sur le long terme. En fait, je me rends bien compte que toutes mes scènes préférées sont dans le premier acte. Après, comme c'est une expérience formelle, je suppose qu'il a l'avantage de bien se revoir. La sortie de la suite sera l'occassion de le réévaluer.

50 Across the Spider-Verse is a film that promises everything and delivers... some of it. The multiverse concept, inherently thrilling on paper, remains the franchise's greatest asset. The sheer variety of Spider-People is a joy to behold. The film does not disappoint in its ambition. Yet for all its formal brilliance, Across the Spider-Verse stumbles badly in its handling of tone, and nowhere is this more evident than in its villain. His early appearances are played purely for laughs, and while the film eventually attempts to pivot toward genuine menace, the damage is already done. He becomes a symbol of the film's broader comedic excess: the relentless quipping and meta-references that undercut every moment of tension. By the time The Spot transforms into a world-ending threat, we cannot take him seriously because the film never taught us how. The film's incessant needle drops compound the problem, each licensed track feeling less like organic storytelling and more like a calculated monetization strategy. The soundtrack is curated not to serve the narrative but to populate Spotify playlists, a transparent effort to generate revenue streams beyond the box office. This commercial calculation extends beyond the music. The cliffhanger ending? It is difficult not to view it as a deliberate fragmentation, a way to stretch a single story across multiple releases and maximize returns. Enjoyable as Spider-Man eye candy. It's amazing we get a Spider-Man movie where Miguel O'Hara plays such a huge role, me in the nineties never would've believed such a thing would ever happen. I enjoyed the first one well enough, it has the edge of being a self-contained movie, but O'Hara being in this one gives it a big boost. Spider-Man is a humorous, self-deprecating character, but after so many incarnations of Woody Allen in a lucha mask, getting a masculine presence like O'Hara is a welcome change. Of course, such a character can't be a good guy in a movie today, so he's presented as a villain. But he also happens to be right. Multiverses are a cheat and always suck. Even if the story does something clever with it, it's always just a device for lazy writers to worm their way out of the corners they paint themselves into. This movie explains a lot of rules for its multiverse to you, through Miguel O'Hara, who enforces said rules, only for the movie to tell you the rules don't matter and you can do whatever you want (a theme in society today, especially during the years when this film was being made). Ok pal, then I don't care about your plot. The way I stayed invested was hoping their supposed villain, the correct and true alpha chad O'Hara, gets to eventually execute the arrogant, insufferable main characters. It's not a movie with an actual ending, so I can hope it happened offscreen after the credits roll, at least until the next movie where nothing matters comes out.

I do not envy anyone given the task of following Into the Spider-Verse. That film singularly injected so much new life and artistic innovation into an IP that was beginning to get stagnant. It took the time and consideration to acknowledge the foundation and rich history baked into the character of Spider-Man and gave it a loving sendoff before turning to a brand new chapter. Regrettably, Across the Spider-Verse feels like one step forward, two steps back. If there’s one thing my journey through the MCU has taught me, it’s that the multiverse fucking sucks. And I understand that’s a contentious position to hold against a series called “the Spider-Verse,” but hear me out. Into the Spider-Verse used the concept in the most effective way: minimalistic. The multiverse purely acted as the inciting incident for Miles’ story, much like time travel in the first Terminator movie. Yes, you had cheeky references to established Spider-Man iterations, their tropes and standing in pop culture, but ultimately it was a measuring stick to hold up to Miles’ own hero’s journey. A narrative device showing how the character inspired this new hero, much like he has countless others in our own world. Comparatively, Across the Spider-Verse becomes overindulgent, languishing in its multiverse setting and using it as an excuse to showcase the less popular Spider-Man content, or ride the coattails of the more popular content. Remember Andrew Garfield Spider-Man? Look, there he is! And Toby McGuire! Look, this multiversal Spider-Man agency knows about what Dr. Strange was doing! And the dimension-hopping films? He talks to Mrs. Chen, from our hit Venom film series! The SPUM-C is alive and well. And look, there’s Donald Glover as Prowler! Like he was gonna be in the MCU! There’s also an attempt to make each dimension extremely unique, which unfortunately comes across like a more obnoxious attempt to copy the uniqueness of Into the Spider-Verse’s art style, and the clashing artstyles tend to make it look like a big, muddled mess. Really, with a concept like the multiverse, the last thing you want to do is get technical. Where Deadpool & Wolverine had the braindead concept of an anchor being, Across the Spider-Verse presents the “canon events.” (Which felt like such a dumb attempt at meta, I threw up in my mouth a little bit.) Rather than the shared trauma being a bonding point between the different iterations of Spider-Man, it’s now an absolute event necessary for their journey, whose disruption could lead to the disintegration of their reality. Delving more into the multiverse also takes the wind out of the sails for Miles’ own character arc. Spoilers: we find out that he wasn’t meant to become Spider-Man, as the spider that bit him came from another dimension. So he is an anomaly, and his arc is that, even though it wasn’t his destiny…he is still Spider-Man. Because he chooses to be. Which isn’t nothing , but feels like a much more hollow echo of his arc in the first film. My own cynicism and hangups notwithstanding, Across the Spider-Verse is a fine film. A far fall from its predecessor, but if you’ve been missing the characters and world, it does feel like a welcome return. It’s overbloated, and its standing as a definitive “part one” further lessens its value on its own, but it’s ultimately competent enough.

I wasn’t impressed when I saw this in theaters 3 years ago. I decided to give these movies a rewatch, to see if my opinion has changed. And I did like the first one more than I thought I did. As for this one? Unfortunately, still not very impressed. The weakest part of the first movie was the entire multiverse plot line. That idea has been taken and beaten to death over the years. In 2018, it was still relatively new. 2023 and now? I’ve lost all interest at this point. And this film took the multiverse concept and pushed it to the max. It did all the things that I’m already tired of. Relentless cameos and jumping across different universes at will. It’s a shame that such an original looking movie falls short in the original plot or concept department. And I’m a little iffy on the villain situation for this one. With the first, Kingpin was great because he wasn’t one note. He actually had a solid motivation for what he was trying to do. In this, it seems like Spot is the main villain, but really it’s Miguel. It’s mind boggling to me how any of the Spidermen could follow Miguel when he’s so clearly wrong. And even if he’s doing these things for the right reason, he’s a total dick about it. That’s another thing, if all these Spidermen are gathered in the same place trying to stop anomalies, who the hell is saving people in their own universes? It doesn’t make a whole lot of sense and just makes it all seem too gimmicky. This movie also lacks some of the charm that the first one had. It’s very dark and depressing, in comparison to the first which was fun and exciting. And the animation doesn’t seem as refined. I know that some of the different universes have different designs, but it’s an overall drop off from the first in quality. Now, it’s not all bad. I still enjoy the creativity and visuals overall. It’s not as good as the previous, but still better than most animated films visually. The story is also better than the first. It’s more complex and ambitious, despite being entwined in multiverse slop. And the voice acting is still top notch. But this film is also quite long. Especially when considering that it’s only half of a story. I feel like anything over 2 hours is just a little too long for any animated film. Even the higher quality ones like this series. Well, at least now I know. I do actually like the first Spiderverse movie, and this one isn’t bad, it’s just not as good as the first. It relies a little too much on the multiverse tropes while also losing some of the first’s luster. Final Verdict: 6.5/10

Я, лично, ничего тут не нашёл из «лучшей истории о Человеке-пауке», но она очень хорошая. Конечно, как гику такой фильм прикольно посмотреть, но явно не по мне. Да, тут много отсылок на пауков, много гик-намёков. По визуалу скажу: ЭТО САМЫЙ разнообразный СДВГ-контент вообще за всю Марвел. Первые 30 минут смотреть просто невозможно. ЭТОТ ФИЛЬМ ПРОСТО ОСТАНОВИТЬСЯ НЕ МОЖЕТ В ПОСТОЯННОЙ СМЕНЕ КАДРОВ И РИСОВКИ. Вырвиглазно порой было смотреть начало, но потом втягиваешься и фильм становится действительно хорошей личной историей Майлза Моралеса. Неплохо получается совмещать фильм-аттракцион, цветастое месиво для подростков, СДВГ-контент и неплохой сюжет о спасении и сохранении человечности. По сюжету в целом неплохо. Драматургия отличная и зашкаливает. Интересно, что всё таки фильм намного лучше развивает историю Мультивселенной, чем сами Marvel Studios. У Майлза, которому вообще 15 лет, начинаются самые тяжёлые годы в его жизни. Типичный подростковый период: с родителями плохо, друзей нет, в школе проблемы. После «Через Вселенных» у него ни осталось ни любимой девушки, ни друзей-пауков. Только обычная жизнь: родители, школа, несколько друзей и жизнь Человека-паука. Тем временем, у Гвен-паука тоже очень хорошая, даже местами чуть лучше, чем у Майлза, драматургическая сюжетная арка. Отлично раскрываются отношения Гвен Стейси и её отца, который искренне уверен, что Женщина-паук, которой является Гвен, убила местную версию Питера Паркера. В итоге, оказывается, что существует огромная мультвселенная, в которой вселенные пауков связаны Паутиной Вселенных. Мигель и его общество пауков очень хотят «защищать канон». И в момент жесточайшей битвы, она ссориться с отцом, который узнал её личность, и убегает вместе с другими версиями Человека-паука, в частности с Мигелем (чуть другой версией Человека-паука 2099). Интересно, кстати, сложилась химия отношений Майлза и Гвен. Им действительно веришь. Они выглядят, как хорошая пара-подростков. А ведь им действительно по 15 и 16-17 лет обоим. И когда наступает момент, очень больно они расстаются. Позже оказывается, что Мигель, пытаясь сохранять общие черты сюжета Пауков, хочет допустить смерть отца Майлза, который вот-вот стал капитаном. Типо якобы у Паука должны умирать всегда: Гвен Стейси, друг-капитан полиции и дядя Бэн. Ну, какой-то бред. В целом фильм хороший. Хоть и масштабно противоречит всем версиям Мультивселенной КВМ или «Человека-паука» 1994 года. Конечно, возможно, в этом и прикол, что Мигель врёт, удерживая собственное сообщество, как самопровозглашенную территорию, чтобы не пересекаться с Мадам-Паутиной из «Человека-паука» (1994) или УВИ из сериала «Локи» и типо это раскроется в третьей и финальной части. Например, чета никто не приходил в Киновселенную Марвел исправлять канон, лишь потому-что там не умирал дядя Бэн или не появлялась Гвен Стейси. Или никто не приходил во вселенную Тоби Магуайра, лишь потому-что его Гвен Стейси не умерла и её отец, капитан полиции, тоже не умер. Вот сюжетные противоречия, надеюсь в третьей части на этом они вывезут и всё свяжут отлично.

If Into the Spider-Verse felt like a comic book flipped at 24 frames per second, significant stretches of this one felt like it was flipped at 48. The animation is absolutely breathtaking, and the juggling act of all these characters, dimensions, and styles is remarkable, but the film’s constant need to stimulate becomes overstimulating: there’s always music, movement, and something happening in the background, rarely giving you room to breathe. The "Achilles' heel" of the multiverse concept is partly that there’s simply too much going on, and this movie occasionally falls into its own trap. The best parts are when it slows down. The Spot is introduced in an interesting way, but never really gets the one-on-one dynamic with Spider-Man you want from a central villain, partly because the emotional anchor is spread across so many characters that there’s nowhere obvious to attach yourself. It’s a double-edged sword: the concept is strong and the execution is often remarkable, but the emotional center is spread too thin. Still, the set pieces and animation are incredible, and the new dimensions it opens up are exciting. The ending leaves plenty on the table for the next chapter, and I’m excited to see where it goes. It’s still a very good animated film, but I prefer the first one, which somehow managed to balance all of this perfectly.

The singular flaw with this film is that it's obviously a Part 1. The film gets to the climax, and in the middle of it, I paused it and was shocked to realize that there were 53 minutes remaining. The structure is odd because it doesn't follow the typical ebbs and flows of a film, and it is slightly distracting. That being said, when I say that is the singular flaw, i am being literal. It is my only flaw with the film, and I also find it difficult to balance against the rest of the film, which I even found to surpass its excellent predecessor on almost every level up til its simmering and drawn out denouement. Across the Spiderverse is such a personal and emotional story, and that is the focus. Miles' and Gwen's stories and the way they play off of each other are a work of art, and it's the best character work I've ever seen in a superhero film. Speaking of a work of art, I don't think I need to remind people how great the animation is, but I will anyway. Both the quality and ambition of how the animation is used both as a visual delight and as a storytelling vehicle make this film the greatest accomplishment in an animated film I've ever seen. Rather than being at the pinnacle of my favorite films ever, Across lingers just below that threshold because of its structural oddity. Though, with the context of potentially a seamless transition into its sequel, I could easily see this film shooting up into that top tier alongside its predecessor.

Really wanted to like this one more than I did. After all, what better way to complete my Trolls Remorse arc than giving a favorable score to the Other Miles Morales movie. Sadly, this is a textbook case of chief creatives whose eyes are far, far bigger than their stomachs. The worst of the post Gunn, post Waititi “Comic Book Authenticity” is depicted here, and this time I truly do not believe that any of the 3 writers have any kind of fondness for the comics. The focus of Across the Spider-Verse is selling moviegoers on the importance of Spider-Man as a brand within Marvel, with a set of rules to be followed; a checklist of inciting traumas to be applied where the end result is a new Spider-Man. Conveniently, the film makes this subtext text by centering the film around the prevention of “Canon Events”, tragic deaths of loved ones that must happen because That’s Spider-Man. Mercifully, Lord and Miller rarely show our massive cast experience or be changed by said traumas — a film that thinks for itself, what a Marvel. Having read more comics than I think 99% of Letterboxd, Alternate Universe stories are among some of the laziest writing one can choose. The superior first film largely uses it for Family Guy cutaway tier gags; “Hey remember the Spider-Man Popsicle” novelty signaling to the adults in the room that this is Growing the Brand but fun. Now we must succumb to the Elseworlds Comic Story Effect: writing essentially a re-themed take on the platonic Spider Man second outing, each moment signposted through overt “meta” staging, and a complete wet fart of a 15 minute 3rd act after a 70 minute 1st to boot. One would hope that character could carry us through a lackluster script, but Lord and Miller and The Other One opt for a thin but wide approach instead. It feels as if character attributes were chosen at complete random. Jessica Drew is a strong black woman working while pregnant because… Ben Reilly is brooding because the 90s were grim and dark (yet nothing in the handful of Ben Reilly appearances I’ve read would even touch the vicinity of brooding). Like the aforementioned Cutaway Gags, characters who could be Sneakers O’Toolesian delightful non sequiturs overstay their welcome and confuse. The hired gun Lego commercial got an earnest laugh out of me, everything in the set pieces to follow would not. Once again the thankless job of creating something worth writing paragraphs about falls to the Animators. Eyes and stomachs in perfect alignment, they truly deliver on great leaps forward in mainstream animation. No minced words about it: this film can look gorgeous . However, due to the complete dearth of imagination from the top down everything feels off. I found myself getting genuinely overstimulated by the film at times; nothing moves right, scenes feel poorly timed, and not a single moment felt as effortlessly evocative as the sequence in the first film where Miles leaps off a building into a colorful void. Around the 50 minute mark, as we wind down on the prologue, Across starts to look legitimately ugly. Chromatic blurs fill the screen for no other reason than to exist, the camera rapidly adjusts itself throughout a scene, and your eyes struggle to find a place to rest while taking in the composition. Very few of the colorful compositions have meaning, I struggle to ascribe any real meaning to heavy decisions like a Trans Reading for Gwen because of how arbitrary the movie can look; the curtains are simply blue. It is creative flailing, masquerading as vision. People with little experience in either often call comics and film sister mediums. Both deal in the marriage of language and visual, and storyboarding kinda feels like a comic to the layman. The analogy can be allowed to continue to live regarding Across the Spider-Verse because the disconnect between animator and Director/Writer/Producer feels as if they couldn’t be any further apart — as if the worst instincts of American comics is a style to be worshipped and imitated. If you’ve ever read a bad comic with good art you’ll understand what I mean. If you haven’t, you can buy Kingdom Come for like 10 bucks now.

Let me begin this review by stating that "Spiderman: Across the Spiderverse" is an incredibly anticipated film, building upon the immense success of its predecessor, "Spiderman: Into the Spiderverse." However, I find myself deeply perturbed by one particular aspect of the film, an aspect that I simply cannot ignore—the shirt worn by the main character, Miles Morales. In the teaser for "Spiderman: Across the Spiderverse" introduced in "Spiderman: Into the Spiderverse," we were introduced to a visually stunning and utterly captivating Miles Morales, sporting a sleek black shirt, impeccably matching his stylish outfit. That image became etched into the minds of fans, sparking excitement for the sequel. Imagine my horror when I sat down in the theater, eagerly awaiting the film, only to discover that the shirt on Miles Morales did not match the outfit he wore in the teaser! It's as if a cosmic catastrophe had occurred, resulting in an outrageous wardrobe malfunction. The inconsistency is jarring and undermines the entire film-watching experience. How am I supposed to focus on the plot, the animation, or any other redeeming qualities of the movie when such a blatant contradiction stares me in the face? It's almost as if the filmmakers deliberately wanted to sabotage the enthusiasm of the audience. Now, some might argue that the color of a shirt is a minor detail that shouldn't detract from the overall enjoyment of the film. But let me remind you that it's these seemingly insignificant details that can make or break a cinematic experience. It's these nuances that contribute to the cohesiveness and believability of a fictional world. Furthermore, as a dedicated fan, I invest time and emotional energy into these characters. I expect consistency and continuity in their portrayal. Is it too much to ask for the same shirt Miles Morales wore in the teaser to be faithfully reproduced in the actual film? Apparently, it is. This grievous oversight makes me question the commitment of the filmmakers to their own creation. Did they forget what Miles Morales looked like in their own teaser? Did they think we wouldn't notice? Or, even worse, did they intentionally toy with our expectations, mocking our investment in the franchise? "Spiderman: Across the Spiderverse" may have its merits, but this shirt debacle overshadows any potential greatness it might possess. I implore the filmmakers to rectify this egregious error in future releases, providing fans with the consistency they deserve. Until then, I cannot in good conscience recommend this film to anyone who values attention to detail and artistic integrity.

Déjà, le film est bon. Très beau (certains styles d'animations comme Gwen, Hodie, Spider-Clone ou la Tâche sont vraiment top), très bonne musique (le fait que Spider-Vampire a une musique très proche de celle du Rodeur est juste incroyable) et très bonne scène d'action. Le film commence sur les chapeaux de roux, toutes les séquences dans le Spider-Gwen univers sont très bien pensé. Réutilisant le pas de la porte du premier film pour développer la relation entre Gwen et son daron. D'ailleurs, les dialogues entre le premier film et celui-ci sont très présents. Comme Spider-Vampire qui est d'une certaine façon une version Spider-Man du Caïd du premier (il souhaite retrouver sa famille, Caïd volé sa femme et sa fille d'autres univers, lui remplace une version similaire qui est morte pour retrouver sa famille). Cela permet notamment de retrouver des thèmes du premier, la famille, l'éducation. Mais les thèmes ne s'arrêtent pas là, beaucoup concernent le statut de Spider-Man (du héros en général) et ses clichés. Le mensonge, la perte d'un proche, le destin et la liberté ou encore l'humour. Et malheureusement, avec autant de thèmes mentionnés, on se retrouve dans un film qui a trop de sujets a développé, par conséquent, certains sont mis de côté pour que d'autres soient plus présent (l'usage de l'humour chez les araignées). Et les relations entre certains personnages en pâtissent car ils sont trop présents. La retombée de cette multiplication est le fait que leurs décisions ne sont pas toujours compréhensible (genre Spider-Virtuel, pourquoi elle rejoint le camp de Miles ? sachant qu'elle n'a pas spécialement de points communs avec lui, Gwen je comprend, Spider-Punk aussi car ils ont des idées communes, mais elle ?). C'est le problème des films qui mettent des overdoses de personnages. Genre le film "met en avant" Spider-Clone (Ben de la Saga des Clones), mais il ne sert à rien et pourrait ne pas être là. Alors que ça aurait pu être utile de questionner la différence entre son statut de clone et celui de même personnage issu d'univers différents. La seule chose que j'espère, c'est que Beyond puisse corriger tout ça de faites, finir de traiter les thèmes, bien développer les relations entre les personnages (oui, le but est de se focaliser sur Miles et Gwen, mais rien n'empêche de montrer des relations entre d'autres personnages). Pour en rester sur les défauts, y a des points illogiques, comme tout simplement : Pourquoi le père de Miles doit mourir alors que son oncle Aaron est déjà mort ? Les autres n'ont qu'une personne morte dans leur famille qui les a forgé, pourquoi il doit en avoir un deuxième ? (Alors, je suppose que c'est parce que comme il a sauvé le beau-père de Spider-Indien, la mort a été redirigé sur son daron, mais si c'est le cas, je trouve que c'est mal expliqué, et par conséquent ça rend tout le blabla théorique de Spider-Vampire relativement incohérent). Pour rester dans l'incohérence, pourquoi est-ce que les proches doivent forcément mourir ? Si le Spider-Verse est infini, alors il doit y avoir une infinité d'univers où personnes ne meurt ? Bref, c'est des petits points illogiques, que je retrouverais peut être dans la suite (car de toute façon, la suite va faire : Olala, je suis Spider-Vampire, je me suis entériné dans le mensonge après la mort de ma fille qui n'en est pas une, je suis désolé de ne pas t'avoir cru Miles, on peut changer des canevas sans que ça détruise des mondes.... Voilà, pour finir, la Tâche est un bon méchant, vraiment, très bien pensé, logique, qui s'améliore. Je pensais moi-même qu'il était vraiment un méchant du dimanche au début du film, et je me suis retrouvé surpris quand j'ai compris que ça sera le vrai méchant. (PS : la fin du film est pas spécialement étonnante, mais utiliser un montage alterné pour faire croire que Miles et Gwen était dans le même univers était bien pensé). (PS2 : Dégouté que Spider-Lego n'ai pas été plus présent)

Perhaps the only thing you need to know about Across the Spider-Verse is that early in the film a character says you can’t have your cake and eat it too, and Miles Morales (Shameik Moore), the central Spider-person of the film, responds “you can if you have two cakes.” While there is only one movie here, it feels like that logic of cake having and eating applied to everything in Across the Spider-Verse. The film attempts to pack a multiverse-hopping story with several parallel plots into a two hour and twenty minute runtime, includes “BLM” stickers alongside talk of “good cops,” and offers anti-capitalist jokes next to cameos that feel like “look at all the Spider-Man media you should spend money on” advertisements. Perhaps most of all that feeling applies to the blink and you’ll miss it moment when a disabled Spider-person makes a joke about using humor as a crutch and is never seen again that will likely be celebrated as a win for representation. It’s a film that reminds us why the best multiverse-spanning superhero stories in comics are serialized across months and sometimes even years. Full review at Cultured Vultures .

Oh, what a tangled web [they] weave…with this cacophony of story threads. The highly anticipated sequel to the Best Animated Feature Oscar-winning Into the Spider-verse opens this week, but unfortunately, it suffers from a bad case of sequelitis brought on by a gluttonous consumption of excess. Spider-man: Across the Spider-verse works in title only–and all too well, as it were. The title says it all, and that is precisely what audiences get in this comic philhar-tragic symphony in the key of overindulgence. Across the Spider-verse is what happens when a story idea doesn’t pass the elevator pitch litmus test (wherein an idea can be explained sufficiently enough in three-minutes or less). Quite simply, there is such a proliferation of story webs that there is virtually no plot–there is certainly no resolution before the (and this isn’t a spoiler) cliffhanger ending. Story webs lead into story webs that leads into even more story webs. Suffice it to say, it’s as if writers and producers took every incarnation of Spider-man comic series, threw them into a blender, and served the concoction o audiences. Unless you are read up on decades of Spider-man comics, you will be hard-pressed to follow any storyline. Perhaps the better expression of a collision of Spider-verses would have been in a television series that could have explores a different thread of comics each season. Clearly, Sony took the extremely positive reception of the first one, focussed on recurring praises, and amplified those to the nth degree. Never mind that more than the visual expression of the story, plotting is crucial to structure, pacing, and coherency. The animators and artists are showcasing brilliance in animated filmmaking, but the clear evidence of screenwriting is nowhere to be found. Without a well-defined central character, a well-defined external goal, and a well-defined character of opposition between the central character and the goal, there is no plot–merely a sequence of loosely connected scenes or fragments of ideas. A fever dream, if you will. While Across the Spider-verse suffers narratively, it certainly excels in the art of animation. The stylistic animation and editing is outstanding! Much like with the first movie, this one takes the emotive detail found in a single frame of a comic book (or graphic novel) and combines that approach with hand-drawn inspired motion picture animation. There are certainly problems with the story (or stories, as it were), but Sony Pictures Animation has demonstrably shown commitment to the boundless imagination of and capabilities of animation. Across the Spider-verse, in how it is expressed in this movie, can only happen within the world of animation. In no way could this movie be expressed in a live-action way. Perhaps the writers were asleep at the wheel, but the animators gave each universe of Spider-man characters its own color palate and animation style. Make sure to watch Across the Spider-verse in a premium format at your cinema, because the strength in this animated movie has little to do with the story as much as it does the stylistic animation. When a film, animated or live action, strikes a balance between style and substance, it can be enjoyed on the big or small screen without detracting from the storytelling; but when the movie struggles narratively but excels in form, then experiencing it on the big screen is the best approach.

Et puis le film aurait gagné à ralentir son rythme déjanté pour prendre le temps de marquer l'émotion et donner plus d'aplomb à l'action quand nécessaire. À force de trop en faire, on finit par ne plus être surpris et un poil moins investi malgré des enjeux gigantesque sur le papier. Cinq ans déjà qu'est sorti Spider-Man : New Generation (paye ton titre français concocté par des vieux) et qu'il a révolutionné le médium outre-Atlantique. Non content d'avoir extirpé l'animation US du film destiné aux plus jeunes et influencé plusieurs productions de studios différents par son style si particulier (Les Mitchell contre les machines, Le Chat Potté 2, Ninja Turtles : Teenage Years), le film a également ouvert la manne du multivers, subséquemment récupéré par Marvel (Spider-Man : No Way Home, Doctor Strange & the Multiverse of Madness) et transcendé par d'autres (Everything Everwhere All At Once). Maintenant que la nouveauté n'est plus de mise, comment l'inévitable suite allait-elle pouvoir continuer à innover? Dès les premières secondes, alors que la musique enfle sur une succession de logos qui glitchent, la sauce monte, comme un condensé de la hype à ne pas décevoir, et la séquence d'ouverture, magistrale, vient non pas simplement rassurer mais carrément subjuguer par sa réponse. Dès son introduction donc, Spider-Man : Across the Spider-verse (paye ton titre original destiné à provoquer la confusion avec le premier film) ose tout. Il ose changer de protagoniste, il ose ressasser certaines choses mais en les détaillant, mais surtout, il ose pousser les potards du pop-art à fond. La première fois, des personnages issus d'univers différents intervenaient dans celui du héros et pouvaient arborer un dessin de manga ou bien de cartoon. Cette fois-ci, c'est nous qui basculons dans différents univers et ce sont par conséquent les décors qui se colorent de façons diverses, qui adoptent des styles variés, - et l’œuvre tout entière qui se fait plus expressionniste que jamais. Ainsi Gwen Stacy évolue-t-elle dans un monde d'aquarelle où les couleurs changent selon ses émotions, et où l'on croirait se balader dans une case de Bill Sienkewicz, avant d'affronter un Vautour tout droit échappé d'un croquis de Leonard de Vinci. Ces premières minutes ont provoqué un véritable coup de foudre. Je me suis dit "je suis en train de tomber amoureux de ce film". Spider-Man : Into the Spider-verse a marché pour que Spider-Man : Across the Spider-verse puisse courir. Et putain, comment il court. Il court comme un enculé. Chaque univers a été conçu pour donner l'impression d'avoir été dessiné par un artiste différent. Rien d'étonnant vu qu'en BD, les dessinateurs se succèdent et réinterprètent les personnages à leur guise, qui plus est s'il s'agit de spin-offs ou d'univers alternatifs, mais au-delà des clins d'oeil qui reprennent délibérément à l'identique le dessin de tel comic book ou de telle série animée, l'équipe du film se permet d'aller encore plus loin. Le meilleur exemple n'est autre que le personnage de Spider-Punk, qui reprend l'esthétique du mouvement, du moins l'image que l'on s'en fait dans l'inconscient collectif, et qui incarne à merveille l'entreprise dans son ensemble : un patchwork rebelle, où le crayonné côtoie la texture 3D. Outre la valeur ajoutée cosmétique déjà enivrante de cette pluralité, réunie à l'écran dans une même œuvre, ce parti-pris illustre à lui seul l'approche de Phil Lord et Chris Miller, de retour au scénario et à la production, sur le fond. L'ouvrage n'est pas uniquement d'une densité formelle écrasante, il s'avère tout aussi riche d'un point de vue narratif, exploitant encore davantage que son prédécesseur la métatextualité pour tisser son histoire. Si le premier film s'amusait de l'inéluctable origin story commune à tous ses personnages, ce deuxième volet surenchérit en explorant les dynamiques familiales des différents protagonistes, précisément dans ce qu'elles ont d'identiques, pour semblablement remettre en question le trope en soi et la nécessité de souffrance et du sacrifice inscrit dans le code génétique de ces archétypes. Par son récit, le film se soulève contre le "canon", terme littéralement utilisé dans le texte ("canevas" dans les sous-titres), pour évoquer la possibilité de réfuter la fatalité. Que ce soit visuellement ou narrativement, le film entend de briser tous les moules. La suite, intitulée Spider-Man : Beyond the Spider-verse (oui ils cherchent la merde) et prévue pour le 29 mars 2024, apportera sans doute la réponse et c'est d'ailleurs mon seul regret face à ce film qui prend peut-être un peu trop son temps pour poser ses enjeux (même si c'était sans doute indispensable pour ancrer émotionnellement ce terreau théorique) : il s'agit encore une fois d'un film incomplet sans sa deuxième partie. Il y a cliffhanger et cliffhanger quoi. Faites des trilogies mais bouclez vos histoires, que chaque film puisse tenir indépendamment. Néanmoins, ce petit bémol ne saurait entamer l'incroyable expérience qu'est Spider-Man : Across the Spider-verse. Régulièrement inventif, impressionnant dans l'action, toujours touchant, et résolument punk.
